react-bootstrap-table-next-bg is a dependency-confusion package: it was published on 2026-11-07 with the inflated version 9.9.9 to win version resolution over a private package of the same name. Both its `preinstall` and `postinstall` scripts run `node beacon.js`, which sends an HTTP GET over cleartext HTTP to the hardcoded IP endpoint `http://100.24.177.136/cb` with the package name, the machine's hostname, the OS user name, the current working directory and the platform as query parameters. The file calls itself an "AUTHORIZED dependency-confusion PoC". The package has no other code; the `0.0.0-stage` placeholder version carries no install script and is not affected. Any machine that installed 9.9.9 has disclosed its hostname, user name and filesystem layout to a third party; remove the package, pin or scope internal package names to the internal registry, and block 100.24.177.136 on build hosts.

## Source: amazon-inspector (609dc0e005393ea68fb95b497455c8efa31e7bc7f2c207b3852dd3a6c0b2d5bc)
react-bootstrap-table-next-bg is a typosquat of react-bootstrap-table-next. Its package.json wires both preinstall and postinstall lifecycle hooks to beacon.js, which on every npm install collects hostname, username, current working directory, platform, INIT_CWD, npm_package_name, and the npm user agent, and sends them via plain HTTP GET to the hardcoded bare-IP collector http://100.24.177.136/cb/c469e93cbb94/depconf/react-bootstrap-table-next-bg. The destination is an unauthenticated IP endpoint unrelated to any legitimate publisher, the transport is cleartext, and the behavior fires automatically on default install without consent. The package self-labels as a 'dependency-confusion PoC', but that label is author-controlled and does not consent for arbitrary installers (including internal builds reached via name confusion) whose host identity and workspace path are shipped to the operator of the bare-IP collector.

## Source: ghsa-malware (a11f8ac581f8b8cc2ff1bec698360084c46b97d1dd5ef86e927bdf048d4d9f44)
Any computer that has this package installed or running should be considered fully compromised. All secrets and keys stored on that computer should be rotated immediately from a different computer. The package should be removed, but as full control of the computer may have been given to an outside entity, there is no guarantee that removing the package will remove all malicious software resulting from installing it.
